{"kind":"reasoning","id":"p6-440f0f26","text":"SID has no audio output (just registers). Good — no audio library needed. The SdlDotNet.Audio using in EmuWin is unused.

Now, key parts:
- RendererSDL.cs draws boxes and text.
- Menu.cs uses Video.ListModes() and Key.
- CIA1.cs uses Key enum.
- Settings uses SdlDotNet.Input.Key persisted.
- Network.cs uses Key + ModifierKeys from SdlDotNet.Input.
- EmuWin uses Events, Joysticks, Video.

So the modernization requires replacing SdlDotNet entirely or providing a compatibility shim. Since the user asks to update to .NET 10 and latest libraries, best approach: replace SDL 1.2/SdlDotNet with a modern rendering/input stack.

Options analysis:

**Option A: WinForms + GDI+ double-buffered Bitmap rendering.** Uses .NET 10 built-in WinForms. No third-party dependency. Rendering: maintain a 403x284 bitmap of C64 colors, scale it with nearest-neighbor into the client area (StretchBlt with InterpolationMode.NearestNeighbor). Text: System.Drawing.Graphics.DrawString with PrivateFontCollection loading c64.ttf. Menu and status overlay drawn on top. Input: Form.KeyDown/KeyUp; translate System.Windows.Forms.Keys to an internal Key enum. Joystick: winmm joyGetPosEx P/Invoke (2 joysticks) with a polling timer. Fullscreen: FormBorderStyle.None + maximized on the monitor. Resolution list in Menu: Screen.AllScreens resolutions or predefined list. This is quite a bit of rework but self-contained, fully managed, and future-proof.

**Option B: SDL3/SDL2 native with a modern binding.** Keeps rendering model closer (surface blitting) and gives joystick/gamepad and fullscreen handling. But requires native DLL deployment and choosing packages. SDL2# (SDL2-CS) latest 2.0.5? Hmm. Also SDL_ttf native. It increases complexity in shipping. And the "latest library" would arguably be SDL3-CS. But native DLL dependencies are a headache.

**Option C: MonoGame.** Larger change, content pipeline needed for fonts. Too heavy.

**Option D: Silk.NET.SDL + custom text via GDI+ rendered to SDL surface.** Mixed.

Given the app is Windows-only (WinForms originally) and its only real output is pixel blocks and text using the C64 font from resources, WinForms/GDI+ is the cleanest "latest .NET 10" modernization with zero native/third-party dependencies (except System.Drawing.Common which is in-box for WindowsDesktop). Input handling is straightforward.

However, the custom C64 keyboard matrix mapping depends on the SdlDotNet `Key` enum in many places (CIA1.cs case statements). We can define our own `Key` enum replicating the needed keys, and map WinForms Keys to it. **What changed**

- [C64Emulator.csproj](C64Emulator/C64Emulator.csproj) is now SDK-style and targets `net10.0` — intentionally not `net10.0-windows`, because the UI is SDL rather than WinForms. Done. The emulator is now a .NET 10 SDK-style project with an SDL3 host.

**Why SDL3 instead of GDI+**

GDI+ is only a 2D drawing API. It does not provide audio, gamepad/input abstraction, hardware-accelerated texture streaming, vsync, or fullscreen display-mode management. For an emulator that produces a raster frame every 19.95 ms and will eventually need SID audio, SDL3 is the better host boundary. The project now uses `SDL3-CS`, `SDL3-CS.Windows`, and `SDL3-CS.Windows.TTF`; the old GDI+/WinForms/SdlDotNet host is gone.

**What changed**

- Converted the project to SDK-style [C64Emulator.csproj](C64Emulator/C64Emulator.csproj) targeting `net10.0`, with nullable analysis enabled.
- Replaced the global `C64` singleton with [C64Machine.cs](C64Emulator/C64Machine.cs): an instance composition root that owns the CPU, memory, VIC, CIAs, SID register file, interrupt line, and emulation thread.
- Made the CPU synchronous: `Step()` executes one instruction and reports cycles; the machine ticks the CIA/VIC by that amount. This removed wall-clock pacing and device calls from the CPU core.
- Added explicit interfaces for the CPU bus, video bus, I/O port, and VIC bank switching.
- Reworked memory into a real PLA-style decode with `HIRAM`/`LORAM`/`CHAREN`, RAM underneath ROM/I/O, character-ROM visibility at `$D000`, and CIA2’s inverted VIC-bank lines.
- Rebuilt the VIC around scanline/pixel output, double-buffered frames, text/bitmap/multicolor modes, sprites, sprite priority/collisions, raster IRQs, 38/40-column and 24/25-row geometry.
- Corrected CIA timer cascades, ICR latching/masks, CIA2 NMI routing, keyboard-matrix scanning, and joystick active-low inputs.
- Fixed TOD hardware behavior: **hours now latch the clock**, **tenths releases the latch**, writing hours stops the clock until tenths is written, and the AM/PM flag now flips at 11→12 rather than 12→1.
- Corrected PAL frame pacing to 19.95 ms instead of a 20 ms approximation.
- Replaced the renderer with [Renderer.cs](C64Emulator/Renderer.cs): SDL texture streaming, integer scaling, fullscreen modes, embedded C64 font, menu/status/FPS overlays.
- Kept the host/client network transport but fixed malformed disconnect framing.
- Removed the legacy `app.config`, `packages.config`, designer settings, `AssemblyInfo`, unused palette/SDL shim, and empty IEC/D64 placeholders.
- Added [README.md](README.md) covering build, controls, architecture, and known gaps.

**Verification**

- `dotnet build C64Emulator.sln -c Debug` → **0 warnings, 0 errors**
- `dotnet test C64Emulator.Tests/C64Emulator.Tests.csproj` → **52 passed, 0 failed**, including the deterministic boot-to-`READY.` test using the real KERNAL/BASIC/character ROMs
- Launched the SDL executable for 5 seconds with a dummy audio driver; it stayed alive with no startup errors. The window/renderer path initialized successfully.
- `dotnet list package --outdated` reports no updates for either project; test tooling was updated to coverlet 10.1.0, Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk 18.11.0, and xunit.runner.visualstudio 4.0.1.

**Remaining limits**

- SID audio synthesis is still not implemented; SDL audio initializes, but the emulator is silent.
- IEC/1541/D64 disk emulation is not implemented. Only `.prg` files can be loaded directly.
- VIC timing is scanline/pixel-oriented, not cycle-exact; badlines, sprite DMA stalls, and advanced VIC tricks are not modeled.
- Uncommon illegal 6502 opcodes are approximate, NTSC is not selectable, and the network protocol remains unauthenticated plain TCP.

The next biggest functional gap is SID audio.

    /// filter. The CPU clock advances the model; resampled stereo-independent

    internal sealed class SID

        public const int RegisterCount = 29;
        public const int SampleRate = 48000;

        private const int ClockHz = 985248;
        private const double CyclesPerSample = (double)ClockHz / SampleRate;
        private const double PhasePeriod = 1 << 24;
        private const int QueueCapacity = 16384;
        private const int ScratchCapacity = 64;
        private const double MasterGain = 0.28;

        // The SID's envelope rates are commonly quoted as times. Attack is
        // linear; decay and release use an exponential curve.
        private static readonly double[] AttackSeconds =
        {
            0.002, 0.008, 0.016, 0.024, 0.038, 0.056, 0.068, 0.080,
            0.100, 0.250, 0.500, 0.800, 1.000, 3.000, 5.000, 8.000
        };

        private static readonly double[] DecayReleaseSeconds =
        {
            0.006, 0.024, 0.048, 0.072, 0.114, 0.168, 0. [… 14,337 characters omitted]             Release = 0;
                Phase = 0;
                Envelope = 0;
                Noise = 0x7FFFF8;
                NoiseBit = false;
                Wrapped = false;
                Gate = false;
                State = EnvelopeState.Idle;
                AttackIncrement = 0;
                DecayCoefficient = 0;
                ReleaseCoefficient = 0;
            }
        }

        private sealed class Filter
        {
            private double ic1eq;
            private double ic2eq;
            private double a1;
            private double a2;
            private double a3;
            private double k;
            private int lastCutoff = -1;
            private int lastResonance = -1;

            public void Configure(int cutoff, int resonance)
            {
                if (cutoff == lastCutoff && resonance == lastResonance)
                    return;

                lastCutoff = cutoff;
                lastResonance = resonance;

                double normalized = Math.Clamp(cutoff / 2047.0, 0.0, 1.0);
                double cutoffHz = 30.0 + (normalized * normalized * 12000.0);
                cutoffHz = Math.Clamp(cutoffHz, 20.0, SampleRate * 0.45);

                double g = Math.Tan(Math.PI * cutoffHz / SampleRate);
                k = 2.0 - (1.9 * (resonance / 15.0));

                a1 = 1.0 / (1.0 + (g * (g + k)));
                a2 = g * a1;
                a3 = g * a2;
            }

            public double Process(double input, int mode)
            {
                double v3 = input - ic2eq;
                double v1 = (a1 * ic1eq) + (a2 * v3);
                double v2 = ic2eq + (a2 * ic1eq) + (a3 * v3);

                ic1eq = (2.0 * v1) - ic1eq;
                ic2eq = (2.0 * v2) - ic2eq;

                double output = 0;

                if ((mode & 0x10) != 0)
                    output += v2;

                if ((mode & 0x20) != 0)
                    output += v1;

                if ((mode & 0x40) != 0)
                    output += input - (k * v1) - v2;

                return output;
            }

            public void Reset()
            {
                ic1eq = 0;
                ic2eq = 0;
                lastCutoff = -1;
                lastResonance = -1;
            }

using System.Runtime.InteropServices;
using SDL3;

namespace C64Emulator

    /// <summary>
    /// Owns the SDL audio stream and feeds it from the SID's bounded queue.
    /// Must be used from the SDL host thread only.
    /// </summary>
    internal sealed class AudioOutput : IDisposable
    {
        private static readonly int MaxQueuedSamples = SID.SampleRate / 4;

        private readonly short[] buffer = new short[8192];
        private IntPtr stream;

        public AudioOutput()
        {
            SDL.AudioSpec spec = new SDL.AudioSpec
            {
                Format = SDL.AudioFormat.AudioS16LE,
                Channels = 1,
                Freq = SID.SampleRate
            };

            stream = SDL.OpenAudioDeviceStream(
                SDL.AudioDeviceDefaultPlayback,
                ref spec,
                null!,
                IntPtr.Zero);

            if (stream == IntPtr.Zero)
            {
                Error = "Unable to open audio device: " + SDL.GetError();
                return;
            }

            if (!SDL.ResumeAudioStreamDevice(stream))
            {
                Error = "Unable to start audio device: " + SDL.GetError();
                SDL.DestroyAudioStream(stream);
                stream = IntPtr.Zero;
            }
        }

        public string? Error { get; private set; }

        public bool Available => stream != IntPtr.Zero;

        public void Pump(SID? sid, bool muted)
        {
            if (stream == IntPtr.Zero || sid is null)
                return;

            if (muted)
            {
                sid.DiscardSamples();
                return;
            }

            int queuedSamples = SDL.GetAudioStreamQueued(stream) / sizeof(short);

            // If the device has fallen behind (window drag, breakpoint, etc.),
            // do not add more latency; keep the current queue playing.
            if (queuedSamples > MaxQueuedSamples)
            {
                sid.DiscardSamples();
                return;
            }

            int count = sid.ReadSamples(buffer);

            if (count == 0)
                return;

            ReadOnlySpan<byte> data = MemoryMarshal.AsBytes(buffer.AsSpan(0, count));

            if (!SDL.PutAudioStreamData(stream, data, data.Length))
                Error = "Unable to write audio: " + SDL.GetError();
        }

        public void Dispose()
        {
            if (stream == IntPtr.Zero)
                return;

            SDL.DestroyAudioStream(stream);
            stream = IntPtr.Zero;
        }
    }
}

SID audio is now implemented end to end.

**Synthesis**

[SID.cs](C64Emulator/SID.cs) now models three 24-bit phase-accumulator voices with:

- triangle, sawtooth, pulse and noise waveforms, including combined-waveform selection
- ADSR envelopes using the SID rate table, with gate-edge attack/release handling
- ring modulation and oscillator sync
- a shared resonant state-variable filter with low-pass, band-pass, high-pass and voice routing
- master volume and voice-3 mute behavior
- real `OSC3` and `ENV3` register reads; unused POT inputs read high
- deterministic 16-bit mono output at 48 kHz, queued in a bounded buffer

The SID is advanced by the PAL cycles the CPU executes in both the live loop and the deterministic `RunCycles` path in [C64Machine.cs](C64Emulator/C64Machine.cs).

**Host output**

[AudioOutput.cs](C64Emulator/AudioOutput.cs) opens an SDL3 `S16LE`, mono, 48 kHz stream and drains the SID queue once per completed C64 frame. Stale queued audio is discarded if the device falls more than 75 ms behind, and audio is muted during fast-forward and while displaying a network host’s screen.

[EmuWin.cs](C64Emulator/EmuWin.cs) creates and services the audio output, and reports a status message without preventing the emulator from running if no audio device is available.

**Verification**

- `dotnet build C64Emulator.sln -c Debug` → **0 warnings, 0 errors**
- `dotnet test C64Emulator.Tests/C64Emulator.Tests.csproj` → **57 passed, 0 failed**
- New tests in [SidTests.cs](C64Emulator.Tests/SidTests.cs) cover sample-rate production, audible gated output, ADSR release to silence, oscillator/envelope register reads, and pitch. The pitch test confirms roughly 24 sawtooth resets per 100 ms at frequency `$1000`, which is 240.6 Hz.
- A local SDL dummy-driver probe opened the audio stream successfully and queued **4096 bytes** after pumping generated SID samples.
- The full application stayed alive for 6 seconds with audio enabled and produced no stderr output.

The remaining fidelity limitation is that the SID is a digital approximation: the 6581’s nonlinear filter, exact envelope-counter quirks, and all 6581/8580 combined-waveform differences are not modeled. I could not acoustically audition the output in this environment, but the generated waveform and SDL stream path are covered by the checks above. [README.md](README.md) documents the new audio behavior.

using System.Collections.Generic;

namespace C64Emulator
{
    /// <summary>
    /// The disk-device side of a D64 image. The C64's KERNAL load path is
    /// serviced by <see cref="C64Machine"/>; this type keeps image, directory
    /// and file-chain state independent of the host menu.
    /// </summary>
    internal sealed class C1541Drive
    {
        private D64Image? image;

        public bool IsMounted => image is not null;

        public string? ImagePath { get; private set; }

        public string DiskName => image?.DiskName ?? string.Empty;

        public string DiskId => image?.DiskId ?? string.Empty;

        public IReadOnlyList<D64FileInfo> Directory =>
            image?.Directory ?? Array.Empty<D64FileInfo>();

        public void Mount(string path)
        {
            ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(path);

            D64Image loaded = D64Image.Load(path);
            image = loaded;
            ImagePath = path;
        }

        public void Mount(D64Image d64, string? path = null)
        {
            image = d64 ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(d64));
            ImagePath = path;
        }

        public void Eject()
        {
            image = null;
            ImagePath = null;
        }

        public D64FileInfo? FindFile(string name)
        {
            return image?.FindFile(name);
        }

        public D64FileInfo? FirstProgram()
        {
            return image?.FirstProgram();
        }

        public byte[] ReadFile(D64FileInfo file)
        {
            D64Image? mounted = image;

            if (mounted is null)
                throw new InvalidOperationException("No disk is mounted.");

            return mounted.ReadFile(file);
        }

        public static bool TryGetLoadAddress(byte[] prg, out ushort address)
        {
            if (prg is null || prg.Length < 2)
            {
                address = 0;
                return false;
            }

            address = (ushort)(prg[0] | (prg[1] << 8));
            return true;
        }
    }
}

Implemented D64 disk support and the menu workflow for mounting and launching games.

**What changed**

- [D64Image.cs](C64Emulator/D64Image.cs) parses standard 35-track and 40-track D64 images, including BAM disk name/ID, the directory chain at 18/1, closed PRG entries, file-sector chains, wildcard lookups, and the final-sector byte count.
- [C1541Drive.cs](C64Emulator/C1541Drive.cs) provides mount, eject, directory listing, file lookup, and file-chain reads.
- [C64Machine.cs](C64Emulator/C64Machine.cs) now bridges the KERNAL `LOAD` vector (`$FFD5` / `$F49E`) to the mounted image. Standard BASIC/KERNAL loads, wildcard loads like `LOAD"*",8,1`, requested load addresses, verify mode, and disk error codes are handled.
- Fixed the existing PRG autostart path. It previously jumped to `$A52A`, which relinks BASIC but returns to the READY prompt. It now uses the standard `JSR $A659` / `JMP $A7AE` sequence, so loaded BASIC games actually run.
- [Menu.cs](C64Emulator/Menu.cs) shows `.d64` images in **Load Program / Disk**. Selecting an image mounts it and opens its PRG list; selecting a PRG launches it. A mounted disk also appears as a shortcut in the file menu and can be ejected from the disk menu.
- [README.md](README.md) documents the workflow and limitations.

**How to use it**

1. Press `F12`.
2. Choose **Load Program / Disk**.
3. Navigate to a `.d64` image and select it.
4. Select one of the listed PRGs to autostart it.
5. Alternatively, after mounting, return to BASIC and use `LOAD"*",8,1` or `LOAD"NAME",8,1`.

The disk stays mounted until you eject it. A game that loads additional files through standard KERNAL routines will continue to find them on the mounted image.

**Verification**

- `dotnet build C64Emulator.sln -c Debug` → **0 warnings, 0 errors**
- `dotnet test C64Emulator.Tests/C64Emulator.Tests.csproj` → **67 passed, 0 failed**
- Added tests in [D64Tests.cs](C64Emulator.Tests/D64Tests.cs) for directory/file parsing, mount/eject, wildcard lookup, invalid images, the KERNAL `LOAD` trap, and an end-to-end boot → mount D64 → launch PRG → BASIC program writing to screen.
- Application smoke test with the real ROMs stayed alive for 6 seconds with no stderr output.

**Important limitation**

This is a virtual 1541 implemented at the KERNAL `LOAD` level, not a cycle-accurate IEC serial-bus drive. Standard BASIC/KERNAL loaders work, but games that install custom fastloaders or directly bit-bang the 1541 hardware will not detect a drive. GCR-level protection and custom disk formats are also unsupported.

The D64 browser starts in the executable's folder, so use `..` in the menu to navigate to wherever your game images are stored.

Yes. In C64 emulation, **T64 is a tape image format**, not a disk image. It is the C64S tape container: a 64-byte header followed by 32-byte file records and the decoded file contents. It is not a raw tape stream, so it contains no pulse timing, turbo-loader data, or physical tape behavior.

If your T64 contains a single PRG, the quickest workaround is to extract that PRG and load it through the existing **Load Program / Disk** menu. No emulator changes are required for that.

To support T64 files directly, there are two implementation levels.

## Recommended: a virtual tape at the KERNAL `LOAD` level

This mirrors how the D64 support now works and is the smallest useful implementation.

1. **Add a `T64Image` parser**
   - Validate the `C64S tape image file` signature.
   - Read the 64-byte header and 32-byte file records.
   - Expose each entry's filename, CBM file type, start address, end address, data offset, and payload.
   - Support normal tape-file entries (type 1); type 2+ are uncommon and not supported by VICE either.

2. **Add a `TapeDrive` abstraction**
   - Mount/eject a T64.
   - List entries.
   - Look up an entry by name.
   - Track a current entry for sequential tape-style loads.
   - Read the entry payload and normalize it into the `[load address][data]` form used by the existing PRG loader.

3. **Extend the KERNAL load trap**
   - [C64Machine.cs](C64Emulator/C64Machine.cs) currently intercepts `LOAD` only when `$BA == 8`.
   - Add a device-1 branch that reads from the mounted T64 instead of the D64.
   - Reuse the existing `LoadProgramBytes` and BASIC autostart path for direct menu launches.
   - That covers `LOAD"*",1`, `LOAD"NAME",1`, and subsequent standard KERNAL loads without emulating `PRESS PLAY ON TAPE`.

4. **Add T64 to the menu**
   - [Menu.cs](C64Emulator/Menu.cs) currently lists only `.d64` and `.prg`.
   - Add `.t64` entries, a tape listing view, and an eject/mount action.
   - A T64 can contain several PRGs, so show them as a list just like the D64 disk menu.

5. **Add tests**
   - Synthetic single- and multi-file T64 images.
   - Truncated/invalid images.
   - Mount/list/read behavior.
   - End-to-end boot → mount T64 → load a BASIC program → verify it runs.
   - KERNAL `LOAD` with device 1.

This would support single-file games and multi-load games whose subsequent loads use standard KERNAL routines. It reuses most of the architecture we just added for D64.

## Full datasette emulation

A real tape device is significantly more work:

- CIA1 cassette motor, switch-sense, and data-input lines.
- CIA1 FLAG/NMI timing for tape pulses.
- A cycle-accurate tape pulse queue and motor state.
- KERNAL tape search, header parsing, checksums, and timing.

Even then, **T64 is the wrong input for custom turbo loaders**. T64 has already discarded the tape's pulse timing and layout. For those games you need **TAP**, which preserves the raw pulse stream. A T64 can be fed to a standard KERNAL tape loader by synthesizing normal Commodore tape blocks, but a game with its own bit-banging loader will not work.

The practical recommendation is to add the virtual T64 path first. It is a modest extension of the existing D64 work and should let many tape-based games launch. Full datasette/TAP support only makes sense if you specifically need turbo-loader or tape-timing compatibility.

    /// <summary>
    /// Matches CBM filenames using the '*' and '?' patterns accepted by LOAD.

    internal static class Wildcard
    {
        public static bool Matches(string text, string pattern)
        {
            int textIndex = 0;
            int patternIndex = 0;
            int starIndex = -1;
            int matchIndex = 0;

            while (textIndex < text.Length)
            {
                if (
                    patternIndex < pattern.Length &&
                    (pattern[patternIndex] == '?' ||
                     pattern[patternIndex] == text[textIndex]))
                {
                    textIndex++;
                    patternIndex++;
                }
                else if (patternIndex < pattern.Length && pattern[patternIndex] == '*')
                {
                    starIndex = patternIndex++;
                    matchIndex = textIndex;
                }
                else if (starIndex != -1)
                {
                    patternIndex = starIndex + 1;
                    textIndex = ++matchIndex;
                }
                else
                {
                    return false;
                }
            }

            while (patternIndex < pattern.Length && pattern[patternIndex] == '*')
                patternIndex++;

            return patternIndex == pattern.Length;
        }
    }

        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Builds the PRG form expected by the direct loader: a little-endian
        /// load address followed by the T64 payload.
        /// </summary>
        public byte[] ToPrg(T64FileInfo file)
        {
            byte[] payload = ReadFile(file);
            byte[] prg = new byte[payload.Length + 2];

            prg[0] = (byte)(file.StartAddress & 0xFF);
            prg[1] = (byte)(file.StartAddress >> 8);
            payload.CopyTo(prg, 2);

        public T64FileInfo? FindFile(string name)
        {
            string pattern = (name ?? string.Empty).Trim();

            if (pattern.Length == 0 || pattern == "*")
                return FirstProgram();

            if (pattern == "$")
                return null;

            string normalized = pattern.ToUpperInvariant();

            foreach (T64FileInfo file in Directory)
            {
                if (Wildcard.Matches(file.Name.ToUpperInvariant(), normalized))
                    return file;
            }

            return null;
        }

            {
                if (file.IsProgram)

            }

            return null;
        }

        {
            foreach (string known in KnownSignatures)
            {
                if (signature.StartsWith(known, StringComparison.Ordinal))
                    return true;
            }

            return false;
        }

        {

using System.Collections.Generic;

namespace C64Emulator
{
    /// <summary>
    /// The device side of a T64 tape. The KERNAL load path is serviced by
    /// <see cref="C64Machine"/>; this type keeps the mounted image and its
    /// program lookup independent of the host menu.
    /// </summary>
    internal sealed class TapeDrive
    {
        private T64Image? image;

        public bool IsMounted => image is not null;

        public string? ImagePath { get; private set; }

        public string TapeName => image?.TapeName ?? string.Empty;

        public IReadOnlyList<T64FileInfo> Directory =>
            image?.Directory ?? Array.Empty<T64FileInfo>();

        public void Mount(string path)
        {
            ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(path);

            T64Image loaded = T64Image.Load(path);
            image = loaded;
            ImagePath = path;
        }

        public void Mount(T64Image t64, string? path = null)
        {
            image = t64 ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(t64));
            ImagePath = path;
        }

        public void Eject()
        {
            image = null;
            ImagePath = null;
        }

        public T64FileInfo? FindFile(string name)
        {
            return image?.FindFile(name);
        }

        public T64FileInfo? FirstProgram()
        {
            return image?.FirstProgram();
        }

        public byte[] ReadFile(T64FileInfo file)
        {
            T64Image? mounted = image;

            if (mounted is null)
                throw new InvalidOperationException("No tape is mounted.");

            return mounted.ReadFile(file);
        }

        public byte[] CreatePrg(T64FileInfo file)
        {
            T64Image? mounted = image;

            if (mounted is null)
                throw new InvalidOperationException("No tape is mounted.");

            return mounted.ToPrg(file);
        }
    }
}

Implemented virtual T64 support and the unified program selector.

**Program selector**

`F12 → Load Program / Disk / Tape` now lists all supported files in one browser:

- **`[PRG]`** — loads and runs immediately.
- **`[D64]`** — mounts the disk and opens its PRG list.
- **`[T64]`** — mounts the tape and opens its program list.

Mounted media stay available from the same menu as **Mounted Disk** and **Mounted Tape**, with eject actions. File handling is dispatched by extension, so there is no separate D64/T64 menu path to choose manually.

**T64 support**

- [T64Image.cs](C64Emulator/T64Image.cs) parses the C64S T64 header and 32-byte file records, handles normal tape-file entries, extracts payloads, and builds PRG data using the record’s load address. It falls back to payload boundaries when the stored end address is bad, which is common in older T64 files.
- [TapeDrive.cs](C64Emulator/TapeDrive.cs) provides mount, eject, directory listing, name lookup, and PRG conversion.
- [C64Machine.cs](C64Emulator/C64Machine.cs) now services KERNAL `LOAD` for device 1 as well as disk device 8. This covers `LOAD"*",1`, `LOAD"NAME",1`, and standard post-boot loads.
- The direct T64 launcher reuses the corrected BASIC autostart sequence, so BASIC games actually run rather than returning to `READY.`.
- Shared CBM filename, wildcard, PETSCII, and file-type helpers were added in [CbmFileType.cs](C64Emulator/CbmFileType.cs), [Petscii.cs](C64Emulator/Petscii.cs), and [Wildcard.cs](C64Emulator/Wildcard.cs).
- [README.md](README.md) documents the selector and tape behavior.

**Verification**

- `dotnet build C64Emulator.sln -c Debug` → **0 warnings, 0 errors**
- `dotnet test C64Emulator.Tests/C64Emulator.Tests.csproj` → **74 passed, 0 failed**
- Added [T64Tests.cs](C64Emulator.Tests/T64Tests.cs) covering T64 parsing, bad end-address handling, wildcard lookup, mount/eject, direct menu loading, and KERNAL device-1 loading.
- Application smoke test with SDL stayed alive for 6 seconds and produced no stderr output.

**Limitation**

T64 is a decoded tape container, not a pulse-level datasette image. Standard KERNAL tape loads work, but games using custom turbo loaders or directly manipulating the datasette hardware still will not work. TAP playback would be required for that.

I did not have your specific T64 file in the workspace, so the parser and load path were tested with synthetic T64 images rather than your file.

The emulator is now a working PAL C64 for PRG files and simple KERNAL-loading D64/T64 programs. What remains is mostly **compatibility and hardware accuracy**, not menu plumbing.

## Biggest game-compatibility gaps

1. **Real device emulation instead of only KERNAL `LOAD` traps**
   - D64/T64 currently service `LOAD` directly from the image.
   - They do not implement `OPEN`, `CLOSE`, `CHRIN`, `CHROUT`, `SAVE`, the status channel, or `LOAD"$",8`.
   - Fastloaders and code that bit-bangs the drive/datasette bypass the trap entirely.
   - A real IEC/1541 emulation is the big step needed for broad commercial-game compatibility. A smaller intermediate step is virtual KERNAL `OPEN`/`CHRIN`/`CLOSE` handling for directory listings and data files.

2. **Tape signal emulation**
   - T64 is a file container; it does not preserve tape timing.
   - Turbo tape loaders need **TAP** playback plus CIA1 datasette timing, motor/sense lines, and NMI/FLAG handling.
   - Without that, many tape-origin games will still fail even though T64 parsing works.

3. **Cartridge support**
   - There is no CRT or cartridge emulation.
   - Start with standard 8K/16K cartridge images, then consider banked formats such as EasyFlash or Action Replay.
   - Many games are distributed as CRT images rather than D64/T64.

4. **Cycle-accurate VIC-II**
   - The current VIC is scanline/pixel based. Badline behavior, sprite DMA stalls, open borders, FLI and some raster tricks are not modeled.
   - This affects both graphics and games that rely on precise raster timing.
   - The next step is a cycle-stepped VIC with CPU stalls and correct BA/IRQ timing.

5. **CPU/CIA accuracy**
   - Common undocumented opcodes are covered, but unstable opcodes, exact interrupt timing and some read-modify-write behavior are approximate.
   - CIA timer edge cases, serial/datasette flags, TOD behavior and paddle inputs need more validation.
   - A standard 6502 compliance test suite would expose the remaining issues.

6. **SID accuracy**
   - The SID is a digital approximation.
   - The 6581 nonlinear filter, envelope counter quirks, combined-waveform differences and 6581/8580 model selection are missing.
   - Games generally run, but music and sound effects are not reference-accurate.

## Smaller but important work

- **Save states and rewind.** There is a `SaveProgram` helper, but no full machine snapshot/restore.
- **Autostart and media swapping.** Selecting a D64/T64 currently mounts it and opens the program list. A “run first program” option and disk/tape swap support would make multi-disk games easier.
- **Native file picker and last-folder persistence.** The current browser starts in the executable folder.
- **NTSC/PAL selection.** PAL timing is hardcoded.
- **Custom ROM and drive-ROM selection.** The emulator loads fixed ROM paths.
- **REU/GeoRAM and cartridge RAM expansion.**
- **Cross-platform packaging.** The README currently describes Windows-only SDL3 native packages.
- **A real game compatibility suite.** The 74 tests cover components and synthetic images; they do not prove that a range of actual commercial games boots and plays correctly.

## Suggested order

If the goal is **“play as many real games as possible”**, I would do:

1. Virtual `OPEN`/`CHRIN`/`CLOSE` and directory/status support for D64/T64.
2. CRT cartridge support.
3. TAP/datasette playback.
4. Cycle-accurate VIC-II and CPU interrupt timing.
5. SID accuracy.

If the goal is **“make the emulator nicer to use”**, the order is:

1. Autostart-first behavior and disk/tape swap.
2. Save states.
3. Native file picker and last-folder persistence.
4. NTSC/PAL, SID model and custom ROM settings.
5. Packaging for other platforms.

The current [README known gaps](README.md#L153) is accurate: the two largest remaining pieces are **real IEC/1541 and datasette behavior**, followed by **cartridge support and cycle-level VIC timing**.

### What `$D011 = $1B` does

`$1B = %00011011`: DEN=1, RSEL=1 (25 rows), and YSCROLL=3. Thus its first bad line—and row 0’s first pixel line—is **raster 51 ($33)**. Row 0 runs on lines 51–58; row 1 on 59–66; and row 24 on 243–250. That is why the usual 25-row setting fits the fixed 200-line aperture exactly. The register bit meanings are documented in [C64-Wiki’s `$D011` reference](https://www.c64-wiki.com/wiki/53265).

### How games scroll vertically

The three YSCROLL bits provide only **fine scrolling**, shifting the graphics by 0–7 raster lines. For continuous scrolling, a game advances that offset over successive frames. When it wraps at an eight-pixel boundary, the game also updates the screen matrix—typically shifting or rotating rows and filling the newly exposed edge with the next row from a larger map. It must update the relevant color data as well; the VIC-II does not move the world map or fetch an extra matrix row automatically. A common approach uses **24-row mode** to provide an edge margin while scrolling, rather than relying on 25-row mode’s border clipping and idle areas. Fixed. The jumps were coming from the VIC model, not from host frame pacing.

Boulder Dash uses `$D011 = $17`: 24-row mode with YSCROLL 7, then cycles through `$17 → $15 → $13 → $11` (7 → 5 → 3 → 1). On real hardware, screen row 0 always begins at raster line `48 + YSCROLL`; `RSEL` only changes the fixed border aperture. The old code derived the source row from the aperture and also applied the 25-row three-line baseline, so 24-row mode compounded both offsets. The visible content anchor moved 59 → 57 → 55 → 55 pixels instead of the correct two-pixel steps, producing the jumps.

The fix in [VIC.cs:548](C64Emulator/VIC.cs#L548) now:

- Uses raster line 48 plus YSCROLL as the row-0 source origin.
- Keeps the 24/25-row aperture as a separate clipping boundary.
- Clips to 24×8 or 25×8 matrix rows instead of treating the aperture as the source origin.
- Leaves 25-row/40-column behavior unchanged.

Regression coverage is in [VicTests.cs:101](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L101): one test verifies YSCROLL 7 aligns row 0 with the 24-row border opening, and another verifies the exact 7→5→3→1 sequence moves two pixels per step.

Verification:

- `dotnet build C64Emulator.sln -c Debug` → **0 warnings, 0 errors**
- `dotnet test C64Emulator.Tests/C64Emulator.Tests.csproj` → **89 passed, 0 failed**
- Six-second application launch stayed running without startup errors.

I could not complete an interactive play-through headlessly because the tape contains BASIC `SYS` loaders and the test harness does not type `RUN`; the timing model is verified against the game’s actual disassembled `$D011` sequence. A quick manual run in Boulder Dash is still the final confirmation that the scrolling feels right.

- **`$D011.DEN`:** for badline eligibility, the important event is the DEN latch during raster `$30`. A DEN write elsewhere does not replace that frame’s badline-enable latch.
- **`$D011.RSEL`:** changes the vertical-border/display-window comparison geometry, not the badline formula. A write before a relevant comparator event can affect that event; do not use RSEL to decide whether `(raster & 7) == YSCROLL`.
- **`$D016`:** XSCROLL and display-mode bits can affect the current line’s pixel stream; CSEL affects horizontal-border comparisons. These are timing-sensitive, not uniformly deferred to the next line.
- **`$D018`:** the screen-matrix base is used at **C-accesses**. A write during the badline can therefore affect later C-accesses on that line; already fetched columns stay in the internal buffer. The character/bitmap base is used at **G-accesses**, so a write can affect subsequent G-fetches, including within the current line. Previously fetched bytes remain unchanged.

Implemented cycle-staggered VIC fetches and bus stealing.

**VIC pipeline**
- Rendering now uses the real raster pixel origin: the visible buffer starts 76 pixels into the line, so screen column 0 is fetched and rendered around cycle 15 instead of at the line boundary. See [VIC.cs:837](C64Emulator/VIC.cs#L837).
- Matrix and color fetches are staggered one column per cycle. Column 0 is fetched at cycle 14, column 39 at cycle 53.
- Graphics/bitmap fetches follow one cycle later, and each cell is rendered only after its matrix, color and glyph data have been fetched.
- A mid-badline `$D018` change now affects only later columns; already-fetched cells retain their data. RAM writes are handled the same way.
- The row counter advances once per raster line for glyph-row selection.

**Sprite DMA**
- Sprite DMA starts on `Y + 1` and remains active for 21 or 42 lines depending on expansion.
- Each active sprite claims its two hardware slots, such as sprite 0 at cycles 57–58 and sprite 3 at cycles 0–1. See [VIC.cs:952](C64Emulator/VIC.cs#L952).
- Badline bus stealing is 40 cycles; each active sprite adds 2, matching the nominal `40 + 2N` budget.

**CPU stalls**
- [C64Machine.cs:842](C64Emulator/C64Machine.cs#L842) now advances the VIC, CIAs and SID by the stolen bus cycles and includes those cycles in frame pacing. The fixed-point loop keeps elapsed bus time, CPU instruction time and DMA time consistent even when an instruction spans a badline.

**Tests**
Added coverage for:

- [Staggered matrix fetch within a badline](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L211)
- [Mid-badline matrix-base changes](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L232)
- [Staggered Color RAM fetch](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L255)
- [40-cycle badline stealing](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L273)
- [2 cycles stolen per active sprite](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L287)

Verification:

- `dotnet build C64Emulator.sln -c Debug` → **0 warnings, 0 errors**
- `dotnet test C64Emulator.Tests/C64Emulator.Tests.csproj` → **97 passed, 0 failed**
- Six-second application smoke launch stayed running with no startup errors
- [README.md:159](README.md#L159) and [README.md:206](README.md#206) updated

Remaining limits: CPU instructions still execute atomically before their stall time is applied, BA lead-in and read/write-dependent RDY behavior are not modeled, and the C/G slots are one cycle ahead of the published 6569 slots to feed the emulator’s cropped pixel origin. Sprite DMA timing is the nominal slot model rather than a full VSP/BA state machine.

    /// <summary>
    /// The clock interface used by <see cref="ClockedCpuBus"/>. Each access is
    /// one 6510 bus cycle; the implementation stalls reads while BA is low and
    /// stalls all accesses while AEC is low.
    /// </summary>
    internal interface ICpuBusClock
    {
        void WaitForAccess(bool isWrite);

        void CompleteAccess();
    }

    /// <summary>
    /// Wraps the CPU's view of memory so every read and write is individually
    /// clocked. Keeping this at the bus boundary means the instruction helpers
    /// do not need to know about VIC bus contention: a read that lands in a BA
    /// lead-in waits, while a write in the same window completes normally.
    /// </summary>
    internal sealed class ClockedCpuBus : IMemoryBus
    {
        private readonly IMemoryBus bus;
        private readonly ICpuBusClock clock;

        public ClockedCpuBus(IMemoryBus bus, ICpuBusClock clock)
        {
            this.bus = bus ?? throw new System.ArgumentNullException(nameof(bus));
            this.clock = clock ?? throw new System.ArgumentNullException(nameof(clock));
        }

        public byte Peek(ushort address)
        {
            clock.WaitForAccess(isWrite: false);
            byte value = bus.Peek(address);
            clock.CompleteAccess();
            return value;
        }

        public void Poke(ushort address, byte value)
        {
            clock.WaitForAccess(isWrite: true);
            bus.Poke(address, value);
            clock.CompleteAccess();
        }

        public ushort PeekWord(ushort address)
        {
            // A 16-bit fetch is two bus cycles on the 6510, so it must not
            // bypass the clock through the underlying bus implementation.
            return (ushort)(
                Peek(address) |
                (Peek((ushort)(address + 1)) << 8));
        }
    }
}

namespace C64Emulator.Tests

    public sealed class BusTimingTests : IDisposable
    {
        private readonly C64Machine machine;

        public BusTimingTests()
        {
            machine = new C64Machine(
                RomSet.Create(
                    new byte[AddressMap.KernalRomSize],
                    new byte[AddressMap.BasicRomSize],
                    new byte[AddressMap.CharacterRomSize]));

            machine.Cpu.S = 0xFF;
            machine.Cpu.P = 0x20;
        }

        public void Dispose()
        {
            machine.Dispose();
        }

        [Fact]
        public void NopConsumesItsNominalTwoCycles()
        {
            WriteProgram(0xEA); // NOP

            machine.RunCycles(1);

            Assert.Equal(0, machine.Vic.RasterLine);
            Assert.Equal(2, machine.Vic.RasterCycle);
        }

        [Fact]
        public void BadlineLeadInStallsAnInstructionFetchRead()
        {
            machine.Vic.SetRegister(0x11, 0x1B); // DEN, 25 rows, YSCROLL 3
            machine.Vic.Tick(VIC.CyclesPerFrame);
            TickToCycle(machine.Vic, 51, 12);

            WriteProgram(0xA9, 0x01); // LDA #$01

            // BA is low from cycle 12 through the 40 AEC cycles, so the
            // two-cycle instruction starts on cycle 55 and ends on 57.
            machine.RunCycles(1);

            Assert.Equal(1, machine.Cpu.A);
            Assert.Equal(51, machine.Vic.RasterLine);
            Assert.Equal(57, machine.Vic.RasterCycle);
        }

        [Fact]
        public void StoreCompletesDuringBaLeadIn()
        {
            machine.Vic.SetRegister(0x11, 0x18); // DEN, 25 rows, YSCROLL 0
            machine.Vic.SetRegister(0x15, 0x01); // sprite 0
            machine.Vic.SetRegister(0x01, 50);   // starts on raster 51
            machine.Vic.Tick(VIC.CyclesPerFrame);
            TickToCycle(machine.Vic, 51, 51);

            machine.Cpu.A = 0x42;
            WriteProgram(0x8D, 0x00, 0x04); // STA $0400

            // The opcode and two operand reads finish on cycle 54, exactly as
            // sprite 0's BA lead-in begins. A write is still allowed there.
            machine.RunCycles(1);

            Assert.Equal(0x42, machine.Memory.Peek(0x0400));
            Assert.Equal(51, machine.Vic.RasterLine);
            Assert.Equal(55, machine.Vic.RasterCycle);
        }

        private void WriteProgram(params byte[] code)
        {
            const ushort start = 0x0200;

            for (int i = 0; i < code.Length; i++)
                machine.Memory.Poke((ushort)(start + i), code[i]);

            machine.Cpu.SetPC(start);
        }

        private static void TickToCycle(VIC vic, int line, int cycle)
        {
            for (int i = 0; i < VIC.CyclesPerFrame; i++)
            {
                if (vic.RasterLine == line && vic.RasterCycle == cycle)
                    return;

                vic.Tick(1);
            }

            Assert.Fail(
                "VIC did not reach raster line " + line + " cycle " + cycle + ".");
        }
    }
}

Implemented BA/AEC-aware 6510 bus timing.

**What changed**

- [VIC.cs:211](C64Emulator/VIC.cs#L211) now exposes `BaLow`, `AecLow`, and `IsCpuAccessAllowed(bool isWrite)`.
  - BA asserts three cycles before badline C-accesses and sprite fetch slots.
  - Sprite 3/4 lead-in wraps correctly into the previous raster line.
  - Reads wait during BA lead-in; writes are allowed there.
  - AEC-low blocks both reads and writes.

- [CpuBus.cs:23](C64Emulator/CpuBus.cs#L23) adds `ClockedCpuBus`, which clocks every CPU read and write individually. `PeekWord` is two bus cycles rather than bypassing the clock.

- [C64Machine.cs:360](C64Emulator/C64Machine.cs#L360) now uses that clocked bus and replaces the old post-instruction fixed-point DMA loop. [TickBusCycle](C64Emulator/C64Machine.cs#L857) advances the VIC, both CIAs, and SID once per real bus cycle, while only the instruction’s remaining non-bus cycles are advanced as a block.

- [README.md:159](README.md#L159) and [README.md:207](README.md#L207) document the new behavior and remaining limits.

**Tests added**

- [Badline BA lead-in and AEC windows](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L273)
- [Sprite BA lead-in and fetch-slot bus ownership](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L303)
- [Sprite 3 BA lead-in wrapping into the previous line](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L333)
- [Instruction fetch stalling through a badline](C64Emulator.Tests/BusTimingTests.cs#L39)
- [A store completing during BA lead-in](C64Emulator.Tests/BusTimingTests.cs#L57)
- [Nominal instruction cycle accounting](C64Emulator.Tests/BusTimingTests.cs#L27)

**Verification**

- `dotnet build C64Emulator.sln -c Debug` → **0 warnings, 0 errors**
- `dotnet test C64Emulator.Tests/C64Emulator.Tests.csproj` → **103 passed, 0 failed**
- Six-second application smoke launch stayed running with no startup errors
- The real-ROM boot probe continues to reach BASIC `READY`

**Remaining limits**

Instructions are still executed atomically inside the CPU core, so their internal non-bus cycles are advanced as a block; stall placement within an instruction can be off near those internal cycles. The existing one-cycle-early VIC C/G slot approximation and the nominal sprite-slot model remain, as do sprite pointer/address quirks, VSP, and border tricks.

The next accuracy step would be to test expanded-sprite DMA and badline overlap, where multiple bus masters compete for the same cycles.

The regression was not the BA/AEC stall itself. Two VIC scroll errors were making the picture jump, and the bus clock exposed them more clearly:

- **Vertical:** In 24-row mode, the renderer clipped at 24 rows (`textRows * 8`), but the VIC still fetches the full 25-row matrix. During fine scroll, Boulder Dash uses YSCROLL `7 → 5 → 3 → 1 → 7`; at YSCROLL 1 the first six scanlines of matrix row 24 are inside the bottom border aperture. We were blanking them, then letting them pop back in on the wrap to 7. The renderer now allows the full 25-row matrix through the fixed 24-row aperture in [VIC.cs:633](C64Emulator/VIC.cs#L633).

- **Horizontal:** The aperture test was being applied to the scrolled source coordinate instead of the output pixel, which made XSCROLL widen the border and shrink the visible area. In 38-column mode it also subtracted the aperture offset (`51`) instead of the matrix origin (`44`), shifting the whole 38-column display by one character. Both are corrected in [VIC.cs:604](C64Emulator/VIC.cs#L604).

- **Bus writes:** CPU writes now latch at the end of their bus cycle in [CpuBus.cs:41](C64Emulator/CpuBus.cs#L41). A VIC register write can no longer retroactively change pixels the VIC already rendered in that cycle; the new value takes effect on the following cycle.

The vertical jump is fixed. The cause was in the VIC’s character-row sequencing, not in Boulder Dash or display pacing.

**What was wrong:** the VIC advanced its video-matrix row (`VCBASE`) every time it performed a badline fetch. Boulder Dash uses a raster split that starts the playfield with badlines closer than eight scanlines apart, in the middle of a character row. Each of those fetches incorrectly advanced the row, so the playfield alternated between adjacent matrix rows — the 8-pixel jump you saw every couple of frames.

**The fix:** `VCBASE` now advances only when an eight-scanline character row actually completes, while a badline simply restarts at the current row. That is the real 6569 behavior. The change is in [VIC.cs:918](C64Emulator/VIC.cs#L918), with the row-sequencing rationale documented in [README.md](README.md).

I verified it against the actual Boulder Dash tape deterministically, not just by inspection: after loading and starting the game, consecutive captured gameplay frames now move exactly **2 pixels vertically per frame**. Before the fix they alternated between 2-pixel steps and 6–10-pixel jumps. I also removed the temporary tracing code used to isolate this.

Added a regression test covering a mid-row raster split, [VicTests.cs:186](C64Emulator.Tests/VicTests.cs#L186). Verification:

- `dotnet build C64Emulator.sln -c Debug` — **0 warnings, 0 errors**
- `dotnet test C64Emulator.Tests/C64Emulator.Tests.csproj -c Debug` — **106 passed, 0 failed**

I did not do a manual GUI playthrough of the game, so the evidence is the deterministic emulator frame trace rather than watching the SDL window.

Now that character-row timing is correct, the next useful check is whether other sprite/raster-split games show similar row-offset artifacts.

Short answer: no, it isn’t cycle-exact — it’s **cycle-stepped at the bus boundary, but instruction-atomic inside the CPU**. That distinction matters, and it’s the main reason the emulator handles ordinary games and raster splits well but would fail demo-scene tricks.

I based this on reading the core, not on comparing traces against a reference emulator.

## What is already cycle-level

- The PAL clock is real: 985,248 Hz, 62/63/64-cycle lines, 19,656 cycles per frame.
- The VIC advances every CPU cycle, renders 8 pixels per cycle, performs matrix/colour fetches on cycles 14–54, raises raster IRQs on cycle 1, and models BA lead-in plus AEC bus stealing.
- Every 6510 bus access goes through [CpuBus.cs](C64Emulator/CpuBus.cs); writes latch at the end of their cycle, so a VIC register write cannot retroactively change pixels already drawn.
- CIA and SID are ticked per cycle by [C64Machine.cs](C64Emulator/C64Machine.cs#L360).

That architecture is why the Boulder Dash row fix worked and why raster IRQ splits land in the right place.

## Where cycle exactness stops

1. **Instructions execute atomically.** [CPU6510.Step()](C64Emulator/CPU6510.cs) runs the whole instruction, then the machine appends the remaining internal cycles at the end. Real hardware interleaves them. For `LDA $D000,X` crossing a page, the 6502 spends a cycle doing a dummy read of the wrong-page address; here the core just adds one cycle. If that dummy read lands in I/O, the side effect is missing.
2. **Read-modify-write instructions do one write, not two.** [asl(ushort)](C64Emulator/CPU6510.cs#L709) and [dec(ushort)](C64Emulator/CPU6510.cs#L813) read the byte and write the result. The NMOS 6502 writes the old value first, then the new one — three bus cycles. Cycle totals are fudged with `cycles +=`, so the instruction takes the right number of cycles but the bus trace differs. That matters for registers with read/write side effects.
3. **Interrupts are sampled only at instruction boundaries.** There is no CLI/SEI/PLP one-instruction IRQ delay, no NMI edge arming, and no BRK/NMI hijacking behaviour.
4. **VIC badline and DEN are evaluated at scanline start**, not on cycle 14 as on hardware ([BeginRasterLine](C64Emulator/VIC.cs#L897)). FLI, mid-line `$D011` changes and DEN tricks therefore don’t behave correctly.
5. **The border is a fixed per-pixel aperture** derived from RSEL/CSEL/XSCROLL, not the hardware border flip-flop. Opening the side or top/bottom border, border sprites, and border raster effects don’t work.
6. **Sprite DMA only steals bus cycles.** Sprite pointer and data are read live while drawing pixels ([GetSpritePixel](C64Emulator/VIC.cs#L655)) instead of being latched by the two-cycle sprite fetch. Missed DMA can’t corrupt a sprite, and mid-line pointer changes affect the current line.
7. **No idle accesses or obscure VIC bugs** — the `$3FFF` idle fetch, sprite pointer quirks, VSP and similar are absent.

## What else is still missing

| Area | Today | Not implemented |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Disk | Virtual D64 serviced at KERNAL level | Real 1541 CPU, IEC bus, GCR, fastloaders, `SAVE`, status/error channels |
| Tape | Virtual T64 container | TAP pulses, datasette lines, turbo loaders |
| Cartridges | Type-0 8K/16K CRT | Banking, EasyFlash, Action Replay, freeze/RAM, REU/GeoRAM |
| SID | Three voices, ADSR, ring/sync, resonant filter | 6581 nonlinear filter, exact combined waveforms and envelope quirks, 8580 |
| Video | PAL 6569 | NTSC 6567 and PAL-N timing/palette |
| Input | Keyboard matrix, two joysticks, SDL gamepads | Paddles, 1351 mouse, light pen, user port/printer |
| Host | SDL window, audio device selection, VSync/50 Hz, menu, network | Save states/rewind, true per-game configuration |

Priorities depend on the goal: **for playing games**, a real 1541/IEC implementation and TAP support buy far more compatibility than perfect VIC timing. **For demos and raster tricks**, the CPU bus cycles and VIC latches are the blockers.

## If you want cycle-exact

The foundation is already shaped for it — there’s no global singleton and bus accesses are clocked. The work is:

1. Convert the 6510 from “execute instruction, report cycles” to a cycle-stepped core where every cycle specifies an address and read/write, including the dummy reads and RMW double-writes. This is the keystone; everything else depends on it.
2. Move badline/DEN evaluation to cycle 14, make the border a per-cycle flip-flop, latch sprite DMA/pointer/data at the real fetch cycles, and add idle accesses.
3. Add the CIA’s one-cycle delayed flags/outputs, then a real 1541 CPU and IEC bus if loader compatibility is the goal.

namespace C64Emulator
{
    /// <summary>
    /// The C64 serial (IEC) bus. The three signal wires are open collector:
    /// every participant can pull a line low, and the line is high only when
    /// nobody is pulling it. The C64 drives ATN, CLK and DATA through CIA2
    /// port A; the drive drives CLK and DATA through VIA1 port B and can
    /// acknowledge ATN automatically by pulling DATA low (ATNA).
    /// </summary>
    internal sealed class IecBus
    {
        private bool c64AtnLow;
        private bool c64ClockLow;
        private bool c64DataLow;

        private bool driveClockLow;
        private bool driveDataLow;
        private bool driveAtna;

        private bool atnLow;
        private bool clockLow;
        private bool dataLow;

        /// <summary>
        /// Raised whenever the ATN wire changes. The argument is true when ATN
        /// is high (released), which is the edge the 1541 uses to detect that
        /// a command has finished arriving.
        /// </summary>
        public event Action<bool>? AtnChanged;

        public bool AtnLow => atnLow;

        public bool ClockLow => clockLow;

        public bool DataLow => dataLow;

        public bool AtnHigh => !atnLow;

        public bool ClockHigh => !clockLow;

        public bool DataHigh => !dataLow;

        /// <summary>
        /// Updates the C64 side. A set output bit with the matching direction
        /// bit pulls the line low; the C64's inverting open-collector drivers
        /// make a high CIA2 pin mean a low bus line.
        /// </summary>
        public void SetC64(byte output, byte direction)
        {
            c64AtnLow = (direction & 0x08) != 0 && (output & 0x08) != 0;
            c64ClockLow = (direction & 0x10) != 0 && (output & 0x10) != 0;
            c64DataLow = (direction & 0x20) != 0 && (output & 0x20) != 0;
            Update();
        }

        /// <summary>
        /// Updates the drive side. ATNA is the automatic ATN acknowledge: while
        /// it is enabled and ATN is asserted, the drive holds DATA low.
        /// </summary>
        public void SetDrive(bool clockLow, bool dataLow, bool atna)
        {
            driveClockLow = clockLow;
            driveDataLow = dataLow;
            driveAtna = atna;
            Update();
        }

        public void Reset()
        {
            c64AtnLow = false;
            c64ClockLow = false;
            c64DataLow = false;
            driveClockLow = false;
            driveDataLow = false;
            driveAtna = false;
            atnLow = false;
            clockLow = false;
            dataLow = false;
        }

        private void Update()
        {
            bool newAtnLow = c64AtnLow;
            bool newClockLow = c64ClockLow || driveClockLow;
            bool newDataLow = c64DataLow || driveDataLow || (driveAtna && c64AtnLow);

            bool atnChanged = newAtnLow != atnLow;

            atnLow = newAtnLow;
            clockLow = newClockLow;
            dataLow = newDataLow;

            if (atnChanged)
                AtnChanged?.Invoke(!atnLow);
        }
    }
}
